# TypeScript — Prerequisites check

**No new TypeScript today.** Debugging is about tools, not language features — so rather than pad
this lesson with a primer you don't need, here's what today assumes and where you met it.

| You'll use | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `async` / `await` | [week3/day3_1](/learn/w3/d3/p1) |
| Objects as options (`{ slowMo: 500 }`) | [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) |
| Arrow functions | [week3/day2_1](/learn/w3/d2/p1) |
| `page`, locators, `click`, `fill` | [week3/day2_2](/learn/w3/d2/p2), [week3/day3_2](/learn/w3/d3/p2) |

If any of those feel shaky, follow the link before continuing — today's tools assume you can read
the code you're debugging.

**Next:** [Fundamentals - Debugging without an IDE](/learn/w4/d1/p2)

# Fundamentals — Debugging without an IDE

A test fails and reading the code tells you nothing. By the end of this lesson you can stop a
test mid-run, look at the real page, and step through it a line at a time.

> **Partly here, partly in your own project.** Some of today is deliberately *not* automated — see the
> warning before Example 3.

## Why this is a Playwright feature, not an editor one

You can set a breakpoint in VS Code, but that's your **editor** doing it — nothing to do with the
test tool. Selenium has no debugger of its own; you borrow the IDE's.

Playwright ships its own, and that matters because a browser test has two things to inspect: the
**code** and the **page**. An editor breakpoint shows you variables. Playwright's Inspector shows
you variables *and* the live DOM, with a locator picker.

| Tool | What you get |
|---|---|
| `--headed` | watch the browser as it runs |
| `slowMo` | the same, slowed down enough to follow |
| `page.pause()` | stop dead, open the Inspector, step through |
| `--debug` | `--headed` + pause on the first line |
| `npx playwright codegen` | click the app, get locators back |

## Example 1 — watch it happen

**Objective:** run the login headed and slowed down, so the failure has somewhere to hide.

This is the one topic where the course drops its headless default — you cannot debug what you
cannot see.

**Expected:** a Chromium window opens, fills each field visibly, clicks Login, and prints
`https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/dashboard`. Total around 4 seconds because of the
600 ms `slowMo`.

**When this is the right tool:** the test fails and you don't know *where*. Watching it once
usually tells you, and it costs nothing to set up.

**When it isn't:** never commit `headless: false` or `slowMo`. Every colleague inherits a window
opening on their machine and a suite four times slower — and CI has no display at all.

**Challenge:** change `slowMo` to `0` and re-run. Still watchable?

## Example 2 — a locator that fails, seen live

**Objective:** watch what Playwright does while a locator doesn't match.

**Expected:** about `4000` ms, then an error naming the timeout and the locator it was waiting for.

The useful part is what you *see*: the page sitting there, fully loaded, with the field the test
wants nowhere on it. That's the moment you realise the placeholder text is `Enter Email`, not
`Enter Username` — a conclusion no stack trace would have handed you.

Playwright's error also prints the locator it gave up on. Read that line before changing anything.

## Example 3 — `page.pause()` and the Inspector

> **⚠ Run this one yourself, in a terminal — not as a lesson cell.**
>
> `page.pause()` stops execution and waits for **you** to click something. In a lesson cell it
> hangs forever; in CI it hangs the build. It is the one tool here that cannot be automated, by
> design. So this lesson shows you the code and the commands, and does not pretend to have run
> it green.

Put `pause()` wherever your doubt starts:

```ts
import { test } from "@playwright/test";
import { loginAs } from "../../_shared/test-helpers";

test("pause to look around", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/");
  await page.getByPlaceholder("Enter Email").fill("leela@gmail.com");
  await page.getByPlaceholder("Enter Password").fill("Leela@123");

  await page.pause();          // <- stops here, Inspector opens

  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" }).click();
});
```

Then run it headed:

```bash
npx playwright test <your-file> --headed
```

**What you get.** Two windows: the app frozen mid-test, and the **Playwright Inspector** showing
your code with the current line highlighted.

| Inspector control | Does |
|---|---|
| **Step over** | run one line, then stop again |
| **Resume** | run to the end (or the next `pause()`) |
| **Pick locator** | click an element in the app, get a locator you can copy |
| **Explore** | type a locator, see what it highlights |

That third one is the reason to reach for this over an editor breakpoint. You click the thing you
meant, and Playwright hands you the locator it would have used — usually a better one than you'd
have written.

## The faster route: `--debug`

You rarely need to edit the file at all. `--debug` runs headed **and** pauses on the first line:

```bash
npx playwright test week3/generated/day3-base-page.spec.ts --debug
npx playwright test week3/generated/day3-base-page.spec.ts -g "Step 2" --debug
```

Same Inspector, nothing committed, nothing to remember to remove. Prefer this; keep `pause()` for
when you want to stop somewhere specific and deep.

And to get locators without writing any code:

```bash
npx playwright codegen https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/
```

Click through the app; it writes the test as you go. Its suggestions favour role, label and
placeholder — the locators least likely to break in a redesign, which is why it's a better
starting point than hand-written CSS or XPath.

## Best practices

- **`--debug` before editing files.** No cleanup to forget.
- **Never commit `pause()`, `headless: false`, or `slowMo`.** All three hang or slow CI.
- **Read the error's locator line first** — it names what it waited for.
- **Use the locator picker** rather than guessing selectors.
- **Watch it once** before theorising; a headed run answers most questions in 10 seconds.

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| CI job hangs with no output | a committed `page.pause()` | remove it; use `--debug` locally |
| Inspector never opens | ran headless | add `--headed`, or use `--debug` |
| Suite suddenly 4× slower | `slowMo` left in the config | remove it |
| Breakpoint shows variables but not the DOM | that's the editor's debugger | use the Inspector for page state |
| Endless timeout, no idea why | never looked at the page | run headed and watch |

**Next:** [Implementation](/learn/w4/d1/p3) — what debugging looks like when you can't reproduce it locally.

# Implementation — When you can't reproduce it

Same tools as [Fundamentals](/learn/w4/d1/p2), one problem they can't solve: the test failed **on CI, at
3am, once**. You can't pause a run that already finished.

## Debugging splits in two

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Fails on your machine, now | `--debug`, `--headed`, `slowMo`, the Inspector |
| Failed somewhere else, earlier | **artefacts** — trace, screenshot, video |

Everything in [Fundamentals](/learn/w4/d1/p2) is interactive: it needs you and the failure in the same room. The other
half of debugging is arranging, in advance, for the failure to **record itself**.

This repo's root config already does that:

```ts
use: {
  trace: "retain-on-failure",
  screenshot: "only-on-failure",
  video: "retain-on-failure",
}
```

Three settings, nothing kept when tests pass, and a failure leaves behind everything you'd have
asked for.

**Expected:** the three lines, then the command.

**The trace is the one that matters.** It's a recording you can scrub through, with the DOM at
every step — effectively the Inspector, after the fact, for a run on a machine you've never seen.

`retain-on-failure` is the setting worth arguing for: no cost on green runs, complete evidence on
red ones.

## The order to work in

1. **Read the error message.** It names the locator and the deadline. Perhaps a third of failures end here.
2. **Open the trace** from the failed run. Look at the DOM snapshot at the failing step.
3. **Reproduce locally** with `-g "test name" --debug` only if 1 and 2 didn't settle it.
4. **Check whether it's flaky** — `--repeat-each=5`. A test that fails 1-in-5 is a different problem from one that always fails.

Most people start at 3, which is the slowest step and often unnecessary. Steps 1 and 2 cost
seconds.

## What a reviewer checks

- **`trace: "retain-on-failure"`** (or `on-first-retry`) enabled — otherwise a CI failure leaves nothing.
- **No `pause()`, `headless: false` or `slowMo`** committed.
- **Retries configured in CI**, so a flake is visible as a flake rather than a failure.
- **Failure messages read** before code is changed.
- **Artefacts actually collected** by the CI job — a trace written to a container that's then deleted helps nobody.

# Practice — Practice

Three problems. No answer key. These are mostly done at the **terminal**, not in cells.

App: `https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/`. Existing specs to practise on live in
[week3/generated/](/learn/w3).

> Stuck past twenty minutes? Back to [Fundamentals](/learn/w4/d1/p2).

## When you're done

**Of your three routes in Problem 1, which would have worked if the failure had happened only on
CI?** Only the trace. That's why `retain-on-failure` is worth arguing for before you need it —
the run you most need to debug is always one you weren't watching.

problems.statement:
**Build.** Break a test on purpose, then diagnose it three ways.

1. Copy `week3/generated/day3-base-page.spec.ts` and change one locator to something wrong
2. Run it normally — read the error and write down what it told you
3. Run it with `--headed` — write down what you learned that the error didn't tell you
4. Open the trace and find the failing step

**Check yourself.** You can state one thing each route gave you that the others didn't. If
`--headed` taught you nothing, you weren't watching the page.

> **Hint** — the error names the locator it waited for. That line is doing more work than people
> give it credit for.

**Build.** Use the Inspector to find a better locator than you'd have written. 1. Run `npx playwright codegen https://test-automation-banking.vercel.app/` 2. Sign in as Leela and click two dashboard tiles, letting codegen record 3. Compare its locators with the ones in `week3/generated/day3-login-page.ts` 4. Note every place they differ, and decide which you'd ship **Check yourself.** You have an opinion on at least one difference, with a reason. Codegen isn't always right — the dashboard tiles are `

` elements, so watch what it does with those. > **Hint** — codegen prefers role, label and placeholder. Where it falls back to something > brittle, that usually means the app gave it nothing better — which is itself a finding.

**Build.** Investigate a flaky test properly.

Write a test that fails **intermittently** — for example, assert on something with a deadline just
barely too short for the real page. Then:

1. Run it once. Note the result.
2. Run it with `--repeat-each=10`. Record how many of the 10 failed.
3. Add `retries: 2` and run again. What does the report call it now?
4. Fix it properly, and explain what "properly" meant

**Where.** A spec in `week4/generated/`, plus a config if you need one.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **No `waitForTimeout`** in the fix
- **No raised global timeout** in the fix
- **No edit to the root `playwright.config.ts`**

Then answer in a comment: *what is the difference between a flaky test and a failing test, and why
does the distinction change what you do next?*

**Check yourself.** After your fix, `--repeat-each=10` passes 10 times. If it passes 9, it isn't
fixed — you've just moved the odds.

> **Hint** — a report that says "flaky" means it failed then passed on retry. That word is a
> diagnosis, not a pass.
